1. Cubicle (11): the black and white mosaic floor, of the second style, adapts to the functions of the environment divided into two alcoves. The threshold is made up of bipartite scales within a checkerboard border of single tiles; the carpet of the antechamber is made of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp with the edge of a black band; the bedside rug of the alcove N has a series of squares placed by corner with a cross in the center and a checkerboard border like that of the threshold; in the bedside rug of alcove E, which is poorly preserved, double meanders alternated with squares with different motifs.

2. Cubicle (11): detail of section E of the black and white mosaic floor, with the bedside rugs of the alcoves, and the carpet of the antechamber. The bedside rug E shows double meanders alternating with squares containing L-shaped motifs and checkerboard.

4. Cubicle (11): the wall E retains, above the lunette, the holes for housing the joists supporting the vault. The wall, still with a bipartite structure, has the imprints of two small paintings in the red panels of the middle area.

Cubicle (11), wall $ with recess for the bed in section E: the plinth is missing, while in the middle area the distinction between the antechamber, with red panels with circumscribed palmette carpet edges, and the alcove with yellow panel, separated by the architectural foreshortening, can be recognized.

6. Oecus(12): black and white mosaic with a carpet of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp and the border of two black bands; threshold with double meanders alternating with concentric squares. Also in this room, the flooring is older than the wall decoration.

7. The oecus(12) is the only room that still retains traces of the pictorial decoration, in particular on the N wall which shows a black plinth; the middle area with red panels with carpet borders, separated by architectural views closed at the bottom by plutei, reveals the traces of the painting with Theseus slayer of the Minotaur, which was counterbalanced by a painting with Adonis and Aphrodite. In the upper white area, with architecture and carpet borders, 1 remains of the apse aedicule can be seen in the center.

8a-b-c. The S-E pillar of the peristyle (10) has been transported to the National Museum of Naples (inv. 9774) because of the particular interest of the scenes of work depicted on three of its faces. In one of the upper panels appears Venus, with a radiated diadem, and a mantle that falls behind her shoulders leaving her naked body uncovered. The goddess, in a pose derived from a Praxitelian statuary type, was depicted as the protector of the city and all the activities carried out in it.

9. Oecus (12), wall N: the watercolour preserved in the National Museum of Naples is the only graphic documentation of one of the paintings in this room. The scene is reduced to the essentials: a very young Theseus, with chlamys and sword, looks towards the now dead Minotaur, who lies on the ground near the entrance to the Labyrinth, built in regular isodomic blocks. The monumentality typical of other replicas of the same subject is completely missing (a reference is made to the large painting from the Basilica of Herculaneum) closer to the original model of early Hellenism in which the hero is surrounded by jubilant young men, among whom Ariadne is confused. 1. Façade E, view towards S-W. On the left, the entrance to the house at no. 23, on the right that of no. 24; in the foreground the fountain with the head of Mercury. The façade shows the opus incertum with a high plinth in black lava, a characteristic technique for the first phase of the house, and corner reinforcements in large blocks of limestone. Between the entrance at no. 23 and the window on the right, the limestone pillar is clearly recognisable, representing the end of the wall between rooms (3) and (24) and marking the original boundary between the two houses. Right at that point a block of travertine is inserted into the sidewalk. Near the entrances, there are still remains of the decoration in the first style, a continuation of the older tuff façade of the adjacent Casa della Fontana Grande (VI 8, 22).

2. Niccolini's drawing of 1896 shows the horizontal orthostats of the first style in much better condition than the current ones. The smooth plaster in the lower part of the wall dates back to subsequent restorations, carried out up to the time of the fourth style. The original border between houses 23 and 24 is also clearly visible in the plaster.

3. Fauces (1), S wall: faded remains of a decoration of the fourth style. Above the black plinth is the middle area with three main red fields, separated by three narrow intermediate fields with candelabra on a black background. In the right half of the wall you can see the repair of a lesion, caused by the earthquake, in bricks and tufelli, covered with a rough plaster. At the points of contact, the plaster rests on the decoration of the fourth style, which is therefore older than the lesion.

4. Fauces (1), floor, section E, with the lava threshold: fine papier-mâché with regular rows of white tiles; at the entrance to the atrium the number of rows doubles. Along the central axis, the floor was subsequently renewed for almost the entire length of the room. About 100 BC.  DAIB 91.2308

5. Atrium (2), E-side. The floor consists of a fine papier-mâché with regular rows of white tiles (c. 100 BC). The edge of the impluvium is missing and 1 two channels leading from the W to the mouth of the cistern are crudely dug into the floor. The marble parapet of the purification opening to the E of the impluvium was also built at a later date. On the E and S walls there are remains of the wall decoration of the IV style, although very discolored. Red plinth and middle area with red main fields in the centre of which flying pairs were represented, now completely disappeared (see figs. 7-8). The N wall of the room is related to a later phase of restoration, perhaps subsequent to the earthquake of 62 AD, and is completely devoid of plaster. Evidently the wall decoration of the IV style is older than this wall.

6. Atrium (2), W side. The channels dug into the floor, in which the drain pipes from the garden must have been housed, are clearly distinguished. The marble step leading to the tablinum (8) has a relief. The tablinum doors were once decorated with fluted stucco pillars.  DAIB 91.2294
7. Atrium (2): flying pair of Satyr and Maenad, within one of the main fields of painting of the fourth style, now lost.
8. Atrium (2): A couple of Satyrs and Maenads in flight, within one of the main fields of the IV style painting, now lost.

9. Room (3), N wall: wall decoration of the fourth style with a red plinth and white middle and upper areas. In the plinth, panels with stylized bucrani alternating with patera. The middle area is divided into two fantastic architectural views. In the side fields there are medallions with heads, in the central field a vignette now no longer legible; however, the excavation diary reports, with regard to this room, the description of a still life with a basket full of figs and pears and a bird (PAH II 4, 188). It is noteworthy that the two architectural views are not symmetrical, as the base of the right one is much higher than the left one.

10. Room (3), floor, detail: lava pesto and fragments of bricks, originally covered with a layer of red, of which remains are preserved. White tiles form a carpet of hexagons, in the center of each of which is a cross-shaped star, formed by four white tiles and one black tile in the center. Late II style or early III.

11. Room (4), wall O: wall decoration of the fourth style with dark plinth and light middle and upper areas. Two red bands divide the middle area into two large side fields and a narrow central one. The same pattern is repeated in the upper area. In the side fields, yellow horizontal perforated carpet edges are preserved. Apparently, the decoration is older than the opus vittatum mixtum pillar located at the S end of the wall, while the corresponding decoration on wall E, which is very badly preserved, rests on the N wall of the room. It is probably a fourth style prior to the earthquake of 62 AD.

12. Room (6), wall N: simple decoration with red plinth and white upper area, without decoration. IV style. For the application of the brackets, holes were drilled in the walls all around at regular distances.

13. Wing(7), N face; wall decoration of the fourth style with yellow plinth and white middle and upper areas. In the plinth, inside the narrow side compartments, are green plants; in the large central field is a rectangle from which horizontal garlands and perforated carpet edges branch off on which peacocks rest. An ochre band separates the hoof from the middle area. The architectural views in the side fields are closed at the bottom by high yellow partitions and support the low entablature of the central aedicule. The entablature is decorated with a frieze with rosettes and a central picture with sacrificial instruments and rests, in the front, on slender stems supported by bulls. In the central aedicule, among slender gilded candelabra and below a garland of leaves, there is a female figure in flight, with chiton and cloak, who spreads her arms and holds a palm branch in her left hand (Victory ?). In the upper area there are airy architectural views with garlands, candelabras, shields and vase acroteria. In the center, above a square, stands a dressed goddess, with a sceptre on her left arm and a patera in her right hand.

14. Wing (7), wall E: wall decoration of the fourth style with yellow plinth and white middle and upper areas. In the plinth, inside the narrow intermediate compartments are green plants, in the three larger compartments are wide horizontal carpet borders and garlands. In the center of the middle area is a small picture depicting a landscape with villas, at the lower corners there are garlands on which birds rest. In the narrow intermediate fields of the middle zone are fantastic architectural views, closed at the bottom by yellow panels. The low entablature of the central aedicule rests on these architectures, in the center of which is a female figure in flight with a drapery stopped at the waist, with a torch in both hands. Above the figure hang three garlands. In the side fields, at the top and bottom, there are horizontal perforated carpet edges and, in the center, erotes in flight. In the upper area, which mirrors the horizontal partition of the middle zone, airy architecture, perforated carpet borders, plant and bird motifs are represented. In the center, below an aedicule with a low pediment and angular acroteria in the shape of a mermaid, is a young naked male figure, probably a Satyr with thyrsus. 280. Cubicle with two alcoves (31). The room, slightly secluded behind a corridor in the S-E corner of the peristyle, redecorated with paintings of the fourth style, has instead fully preserved the architectural structure and the refined floor decoration of the Republican age, whose partition emphasizes the plan of the room. In the antechamber, the area left free from the beds contains a thick mixture of polychrome limestone flakes within a border of black tesserae and a high marginal flounce of white tesserae. lla. Cubicle (3), N wall: the detail of the upper area, consisting of two rows of ashlars between two lower friezes (white and yellow) and an upper one (blue) and two dentilled cornices, highlights the accuracy of the execution of the stucco relief cladding, the oldest type of decoration attested in Pompeii (I style), similar to that attested in the Mediterranean area since the classical age. The "architectural" structure that is the basis of this type of covering, in which the decorative aspect results from the elegance of the combination of the various areas of the wall and the care of the execution, contrasts sharply with the type of decoration which, in conjunction with the deduction of the Roman colony, is attested on the walls of Pompeii (II style).
